561.title: Forgiver of sin, accepter of return
561.hook: the surah opens with names: forgiver of sin, accepter of repentance (40:3)
561.howItsDone: Muslims call on Allah as al-Ghafur and at-Tawwab in their prayers, and many say astaghfirullah repeatedly each day, following the Prophet's practice of seeking forgiveness often.

segments.voice: Yesterday, led in groups, and your line was greeted with peace. Did you greet someone first, and mean it? Today, a new surah, Ghafir, the Forgiver. Day five hundred sixty-one.

When you meet someone important, the introduction often tells you what to expect. Doctor so-and-so, head of surgery. Judge so-and-so. A title says how they'll treat you. Surah forty begins with an introduction like that. After two opening letters, Ha Mim, and a line saying the book comes from Allah, the Mighty, the Knowing, it lists four titles in a row. And the order, and the balance between them, says a great deal about who's being introduced. The first one gives the surah its name.

Verse three. Pickthall: "The Forgiver of sin, the Acceptor of repentance, the Stern in punishment, the Bountiful." In Arabic: ghafiri'dh-dhanb, wa qabili't-tawb, shadidi'l-'iqab, dhi't-tawl. Count them. Two names about mercy. Then one about severity. Then one about generosity. By the time severity is named, mercy has been named twice, and generosity has the last word. Ghafir, forgiver, comes from a root that means to cover. A mighfar is a helmet, the thing that covers and protects the head. So forgiving, in this word, is covering a sin so that it doesn't harm you. Qabil at-tawb: the one who accepts the return. Tawb is turning back. And qabil is the one who accepts, who takes what is brought to him. Commentators note the two titles are close but not the same: one covers what was done, the other accepts the person who comes back. Then the verse ends: there is no god but Him, and to Him is the journey. Everyone is traveling the same way, toward Him. A few verses later comes an image that's easy to miss. Verse seven: the angels who carry the Throne, and those around it, glorify their Lord and ask forgiveness for the believers. They say: our Lord, You encompass all things in mercy and knowledge, so forgive those who turn back and follow Your way. So the surah opens by introducing a Forgiver, and then shows angels praying for those who return. The surah has two names: some call it Ghafir, the Forgiver, and some call it Al-Mu'min, the Believer, after tomorrow's story.
screen: `TWO NAMES OF MERCY, ONE OF SEVERITY.`

segments.voice: The practice: repent of one thing. Sit, and let your breath settle. Choose one specific thing, not your whole life, one thing, that you'd like to turn back from. Name it to yourself honestly. If you pray, you can say astaghfirullah, I ask Allah's forgiveness, and picture the turning being accepted. If not, simply decide one way to set it right. Then sit in the quiet after the turning. The bell holds the time.
Forgiver of sin. Ghafir adh-dhanb, the first title in Surah Ghafir: the One who covers sin, beside the Accepter of return. Today's word.
Your line: he accepts the return. Today, when someone comes back to you after a mistake, accept it warmly, without making them earn it twice. Day five hundred sixty-one.

562.title: The believer in Pharaoh's house
562.hook: a man of Pharaoh's family who hid his faith speaks up for Musa (40:28)
562.howItsDone: Muslim teachers often cite the believer of Pharaoh's family as an example of wise, courageous speech, and many recite his words 'I entrust my affair to Allah' (40:44) in times of fear.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Forgiver of sin, and your line was he accepts the return. Did you receive someone's turning back like a gift? Day five hundred sixty-two.

Pharaoh's court. The decision is nearly made. Pharaoh says: let me kill Musa, and let him call on his Lord. I'm afraid he'll change your religion, or spread corruption in the land. The advisers are nodding. It's the kind of room where disagreeing could cost you everything. And then a voice speaks up from inside the circle. Not an outsider, not one of Musa's people. A member of Pharaoh's own family. He has kept his faith hidden for who knows how long. Today, he can't keep quiet anymore.

Surah Ghafir, verse twenty-eight. Pickthall: "And a believing man of Pharaoh's family, who hid his faith, said: Would ye kill a man because he saith: My Lord is Allah". This is why some call the surah Al-Mu'min, the Believer. He's never named. Listen to how carefully he argues. He doesn't announce his faith. He asks a question. Would you kill a man just for saying my Lord is Allah? Then he reasons with them on their own terms. If he's lying, his lie is on him. If he's telling the truth, some of what he warns you about will reach you. You lose nothing by leaving him alone. He's not grandstanding. He's trying to save a life in a room that doesn't want to hear it. And he keeps going, over many verses. He reminds them of nations destroyed before them. He tells them about Yusuf, who came to Egypt long before and was doubted too. He calls them to salvation while they call him to the fire. And finally, verse forty-four, he says: you'll remember what I'm telling you, and I entrust my affair to Allah. Verse forty-five: so Allah protected him from the evils they plotted. A moment in the life of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ echoes this. Bukhari reports that when a man in Mecca attacked him as he prayed and began to choke him, Abu Bakr pushed the man away and said these same words: would you kill a man because he says my Lord is Allah? One voice, inside the room, can be enough to stop the room.
screen: `WOULD YOU KILL A MAN FOR THIS?`

segments.voice: The practice: speak up quietly for someone. Sit, and think of a room you're often in, a team, a family chat, a group of friends, where someone gets talked about unfairly. Picture yourself saying one calm sentence for them. Not a speech. A question, like his: is that really fair? Hear how it sounds. Then entrust the rest, to God if you pray, or simply let it go. The bell holds the time.
The believer in Pharaoh's house. An unnamed man of Pharaoh's family who hid his faith, and spoke up to save Musa's life. Today's word.
screen: `THE BELIEVER IN PHARAOH'S HOUSE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: one voice inside. Today, when a room turns against someone who isn't there, be the one calm question from inside it. Day five hundred sixty-two.

563.title: Call on Me
563.hook: your Lord said, call on Me and I will answer (40:60)
563.howItsDone: Muslims make du'a at any time and in any language, often raising their hands, and especially after prayers, in the last third of the night, and between the call to prayer and its start.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the believer in Pharaoh's house, and your line was one voice inside. Did you get to be the calm question in a room? Day five hundred sixty-three.

There's a kind of person who'd rather drive in circles for half an hour than stop and ask for directions. Or carry a heavy couch up three flights alone rather than text a neighbor. Or sit with a problem for months rather than say the words, I need help. It's not that they can't ask. Something in them won't. Back on day one hundred thirty, this path met du'a, the open, anytime prayer of asking. Today's verse comes back to it from the other side: what it says about the person who won't ask.

Surah Ghafir, verse sixty. Pickthall: "And your Lord hath said: Pray unto me and I will hear your prayer. Lo! those who scorn My service, they will enter hell, disgraced." Hear the two halves together. The first is an invitation and a promise: ud'uni, call on Me, astajib lakum, I will answer you. The second is a warning, and here's the surprise: it isn't aimed at people who ask for the wrong things. It's aimed at those too proud. The Arabic is yastakbiruna, from kibr, the same pride the Qur'an names when Iblis refused to bow. Too proud for what? 'an 'ibadati, for My worship. The verse begins with asking and ends with worship, as if they were the same thing. And the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ read it that way. In Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi, he says du'a is worship, and recites this very verse. So, in this verse, not asking isn't a sign of strength. It can be pride. There's a hadith in al-Tirmidhi that puts it sharply: whoever doesn't ask Allah, Allah is displeased with him. People tire of being asked. In this hadith, it's the not-asking that displeases. When someone asks, they admit they need, and the hadith counts that asking as worship. So the verse turns the couch-carrying instinct upside down. In it, asking isn't weakness to be avoided. It's the invitation.

The practice: make a du'a, trusting the answer. Sit, and notice one thing you've been carrying alone, too proud or too tired to ask for help with. If you pray, ask Allah for it now, plainly, in your own words, and let go of how the answer will come. If you don't pray, simply name the need out loud, to yourself, and think of one person you could ask. Either way, sit with the asking done. The bell holds the time.
Call on Me. Ghafir sixty: call on Me and I will answer you, with a warning for those too proud to ask, because asking is worship. Today's word.
Your line: call, and be answered. Today, ask for one thing you'd normally carry alone, from God if you pray, and from one person either way. Day five hundred sixty-three.

564.title: Repel with better
564.hook: repel evil with what is better, and your enemy may become a close friend (41:34)
564.howItsDone: Muslim teachers often cite 41:34 together with stories of the Prophet's patience toward people who wronged him, as guidance for answering insults and family quarrels with kindness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, call on Me, and your line was call, and be answered. Did you ask for one thing you'd usually carry alone? Today, a new surah, Fussilat. Day five hundred sixty-four.

A man from the desert catches up with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, grabs his cloak, and yanks it so hard the thick border leaves a mark where his neck meets his shoulder. Then he says, give me some of the wealth of Allah that you have. Anas is walking beside him, and he says the Prophet turned to the man, and smiled. Then he ordered that the man be given something. Teachers often set that scene, from Sahih al-Bukhari, beside a verse in Surah Fussilat. Today we read the verse.

Surah forty-one, verse thirty-four. Pickthall: "The good deed and the evil deed are not alike. Repel the evil deed with one which is better, then lo! he, between whom and thee there was enmity (will become) as though he was a bosom friend." Start with the first line. Good and evil aren't the same. Obvious, but it matters: the verse isn't saying harm doesn't count. Then the instruction: idfa', push back. It's an active verb. You do respond. But with what? Bi'llati hiya ahsan, with what is better. Not just good. Better. Better than what was done to you, and better than what you were about to do back. Then the promise, and the word for friend is striking. Waliyyun hamim. Hamim is also the word for something hot. A warm friend, a close friend, someone whose friendship has heat in it. The enemy doesn't just stop being an enemy. He might become that. Notice the as though in Pickthall's wording: a likeness, not a guarantee. Then verse thirty-five is honest about how hard this is. Only the patient are given it, and only someone with a great share of good. Ibn 'Abbas is reported to have explained it this way: Allah commands patience at anger, gentleness at ignorance, and forgiveness at harm, and when people do that, their enemy submits to them like a close friend. Fussilat means explained in detail. This is one of the details: what to do when someone yanks the cloak.

The practice: answer a hurt with kindness. Sit, and bring to mind a small recent hurt, a sharp message, a slight, a door shut in your face. Feel the reply you wanted to give. Now look for the better one. Not giving in, not pretending it didn't happen. Just better. A kind word, a small gift, a calm answer, a smile. Picture yourself doing it. Notice what happens in your chest. The bell holds the time.
Repel with better. Fussilat thirty-four: push back against harm with what is better, and the enemy may become a warm friend. Today's word.
Your line: repel with better. Today, when someone hands you something sharp, give back one thing better than what they gave. Day five hundred sixty-four.

565.title: Standing firm
565.hook: those who say our Lord is Allah and then stand firm, the angels descend on them: don't fear (41:30)
565.tomorrow: Signs in the horizons and in themselves
565.howItsDone: Muslims often quote the hadith 'say: I believe in Allah, then be steadfast' as a summary of the faith, and value small, regular acts of worship kept up over time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, repel with better, and your line was the same. Did someone hand you something sharp, and did you find something better to give back? Day five hundred sixty-five.

A companion named Sufyan ibn 'Abdullah comes to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ with a request. Tell me something about Islam, he says, that I'll never need to ask anyone else about. One thing. Something to hold for the rest of my life. It's a big ask, and the answer, recorded in Sahih Muslim, is just two short sentences. The second one is a single word in Arabic, and it's the word Surah Fussilat puts at the center of today's verse.

Here's the answer. Say: I believe in Allah. Then be steadfast. Qul amantu billah, thumma staqim. Now hear Fussilat, verse thirty. Pickthall: "Lo! those who say: Our Lord is Allah, and afterward are upright, the angels descend upon them, saying: Fear not nor grieve, but hear good tidings of the paradise which ye are promised." The same two steps. Say it. Then stand firm. The word is istiqamah, from a root meaning to stand up straight, to be upright, like a pole that doesn't lean. Back on day four hundred thirty-three, we heard a report from Ibn 'Abbas that a command to stand firm, in Surah Hud, was harder on the Prophet than any other verse. Fussilat shows what's on the other side of it. Notice the order: the saying is quick, one sentence. The standing firm takes the rest of your life. Early Muslims explained it in their own ways. Abu Bakr is reported to have said it means not turning to anything besides Allah. 'Umar is reported to have said: stand straight on what you're commanded, and don't dodge around like a fox. And then the reward is not first a prize, but a presence. The angels descend, the verse says. Commentators say at death; some add the grave and the day of rising. And their first words are: don't be afraid, and don't grieve. In the verse, that's what follows steadiness: company in hard places, and two burdens lifted, the fear of what's coming and the grief for what's gone. A hadith in Bukhari adds the practical key: the deeds Allah loves most are the ones done constantly, even if they're small.

The practice: keep one practice steady. Sit up straight, spine upright, like a pole that doesn't lean. Breathe. Choose one small practice you already do, or this path itself, and decide to keep it going this week, every day, even on the days it feels like nothing. Make it small enough that you can't fail. Picture yourself doing it on your worst day. If you pray, ask for steadiness. The bell holds the time.
Istiqamah. Standing firm, upright, steadfast: what comes after saying our Lord is Allah, and what the angels meet with don't fear, don't grieve. Today's word.
Your line: say it, then stand firm. Today, do your one small practice even if you don't feel like it, and notice that doing it is the whole point. Day five hundred sixty-five.

566.title: Signs in the horizons and in themselves
566.word: Signs in the horizons and in themselves
566.hook: We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves (41:53)
566.carry: signs out there, signs in here
566.howItsDone: Muslims practice tafakkur, reflection on creation and on the self, as a form of worship, and use the same word, ayah, for a verse of the Qur'an and a sign in the world.

segments.voice: Yesterday, standing firm, istiqamah, and your line was say it, then stand firm. Did you keep your one small practice, even without feeling it? Day five hundred sixty-six.

Stand at the edge of a wide view, a coastline, a desert, a city at night from a high window, and you can feel yourself get small. Now close your eyes and feel your heartbeat, the breath going in and out without your asking, the strange fact that you're aware of any of it. That gets large in a different way. Two directions to look: out, as far as the eye goes, and in, as deep as you can go. Near its close, one verse before the last, Surah Fussilat points both ways at once.

Verse fifty-three. Pickthall: "We shall show them Our portents on the horizons and within themselves until it will be manifest unto them that it is the Truth." Portents, in Pickthall's English, is the Arabic ayat, signs. And ayat is also the word for the verses of the Qur'an. A verse is a sign. A sunset is a sign. Your own heartbeat is a sign. The same word covers all three. Then the two places. Al-afaq, the horizons: the far edges of the world, everything out there. And anfusihim, themselves: the inner world, the body, the mind, the soul. The verse says the signs will keep being shown, in both directions, until it becomes clear that this is the truth. What exactly are these signs? Commentators differ. Some early scholars read the horizons as the lands that would open to the Muslims and the selves as events in Mecca itself: history as a sign. Many later scholars read it as the cosmos and the human being: nature as a sign. The verse holds both. And Surah adh-Dhariyat says something similar: in the earth are signs for the certain, and in yourselves; do you not see? The verse ends with a question: isn't it enough that your Lord is witness over everything? So the signs aren't a puzzle to be solved once. They're shown, again and again, to anyone looking. Out at the horizon, in at the heartbeat, and down at the page.

The practice: look outside, then inside. If you can, look out a window, or step outside. Find the farthest thing you can see, a tree line, a rooftop, a cloud. Rest your eyes on it for a few breaths. Then close your eyes, and turn the looking inward. Feel your breath, your heartbeat, the fact that you're noticing at all. Move between the two, slowly, out and in. The bell holds the time.
Signs in the horizons and in themselves. Fussilat fifty-three: Allah's signs, ayat, shown out at the edges of the world and within the self. Today's word.

567.title: Nothing like Him
567.hook: there is nothing like unto Him, and He is the Hearing, the Seeing (42:11)
567.howItsDone: Muslims do not make images of God; mosques are decorated with calligraphy and geometric pattern, and 42:11 and Surah al-Ikhlas are central to how Muslim theology speaks about Allah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, signs in the horizons and in themselves, and your line was signs out there, signs in here. Which sign did you catch, outside or in? Today ends the week, and opens Surah Ash-Shura. Day five hundred sixty-seven.

Count the pairs in the room you're in. Two shoes. Two hands. Socks, earrings, chairs around a table. Look outside: male and female birds, day and night, hot and cold. Most things you can name have a match somewhere, a twin, a counterpart, something they're like. Try to name one thing that has no likeness anywhere. It's harder than it sounds. Surah Ash-Shura, verse eleven, sets up that exercise, then gives its answer.

Verse eleven begins with creation. The Originator of the heavens and the earth. He made for you mates from among yourselves, and for the cattle, mates. Pairs, everywhere, multiplying. Then, against all those pairs, the line. Pickthall: "Naught is as His likeness; and He is the Hearer, the Seer." Laysa ka-mithlihi shay'. We met this verse on day two hundred forty-eight, for its last two names. Today, the first half. Look closely at the Arabic. Ka means like. Mithl also means like. Both are there: literally, there is nothing like His like. Grammarians have discussed why. Some say the doubled word is emphasis, like saying nothing, nothing at all, is like Him. Others read it as: there isn't even anything like something like Him. Either way, the sentence closes every door to comparison twice. Surah al-Ikhlas says it in one short line. Pickthall: "And there is none comparable unto Him." So everything in the world has a pair, and the One who made the pairs has none. Muslims make no pictures of God, and mosques are adorned with calligraphy and pattern instead. Muslim theologians have discussed at length how to speak about Allah at all. Different schools drew the lines in different places, with this verse in view. Then the verse does something gentle. Right after saying nothing is like Him, it says He hears and He sees. Beyond every picture, and still listening.

The practice: sit with what can't be pictured. Close your eyes. Notice how the mind reaches for an image whenever it thinks of anything: a face, a light, a shape. Let each image come, and gently set it down: not that, not that. Don't try to fill the space with something better. Just rest in the not-picturing. If you pray, you might rest in the verse: nothing is like Him, and He hears. The bell holds the time.
Nothing like Him. Laysa ka-mithlihi shay': in a world made of pairs, the One with no likeness, who still hears and sees. Today's word.

Your line: nothing like him. Today, notice the pairs: shoes, hands, birds, days. Each one is a quiet reminder of the One who has none. Day five hundred sixty-seven, and the end of a week: the Forgiver of sin, the hidden believer, call on Me, repel with better, standing firm, the signs, and the One with no likeness.

all Muslim schools drew the lines about Allah's attributes in the same place
they differed on how to read the attributes, with this verse in view.

fork.setup: the verse has just described creation in pairs: mates for people, mates for cattle. what comes next?
options: and Allah too has a pair.
pairs are the secret of the world.
fork.reveal: nothing is like Him, and He is the Hearer, the Seer: everything has a pair, and its Maker has none.

original.note: Arabic: there is nothing like His likeness, with like said twice (ka, mithl).

trapdoor: what you thought: God is very great.
what it means: in a world where everything has a pair, Allah has no likeness at all, and still hears and sees.

what a scholar hears: the doubled comparison (ka + mithl) is read as emphasis or as negating even a likeness of a likeness; the verse anchors tanzih, while schools of kalam differed on reading the attributes.

sources.ref: Arabic grammar and tafsir on the kaf in ka-mithlihi
